title: Lemon Drizzle Cake
subtitle: a tender loaf cake soaked with sharp lemon syrup
excerpt: The drizzle is what makes this cake. A lemon and sugar syrup poured over the hot cake soaks in and forms a crackly, sweet-sharp crust as it cools. The cake itself is simple, but the drizzle is the point.
sourceNotes: A British baking classic. One of the most consistently popular homemade cakes in Britain.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the drizzle. Drizzle when defrosted and still slightly warm.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps well for 3 days in an airtight tin. The drizzle preserves the moisture.

content.text: Pour the drizzle over the cake while it is still hot and in the tin. Use a skewer to poke holes all over so it soaks in deeply rather than pooling on the surface. Leave it completely cool before removing from the tin -- the syrup needs time to set.

items.prepNote: zest of both for the batter, juice of both for the drizzle

content.text: Heat the oven to 160C fan (180C conventional). Grease and line a 900g loaf tin.
Beat the softened butter with the 175g caster sugar and lemon zest until light and fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time.
Fold in the flour and baking powder, then the milk. Pour into the prepared tin. Bake for 45 to 50 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
While the cake bakes, mix the lemon juice with the 75g caster sugar to make the drizzle. Do not dissolve it -- the undissolved sugar creates the crackly crust.
As soon as the cake comes out of the oven, poke holes all over with a skewer. Pour the drizzle over slowly, letting it soak in. Leave in the tin to cool completely before slicing.

items.symptom: Drizzle sits on top and doesn't soak in
items.cause: Not enough holes, or the cake was cool before drizzling.
items.fix: Poke holes right to the bottom of the cake. Drizzle immediately when the cake is at its hottest.

items.symptom: Cake has a split down the centre
items.cause: This is correct and expected -- a crack along the top of a loaf cake is a good sign.
items.fix: Nothing to fix. The crack allows the loaf to rise evenly and is a mark of a proper loaf cake.

content.text: The lemon drizzle cake is one of Britain's most popular homemade cakes. It requires no decoration, no frosting, and no complex technique. It is a cake for weekdays as much as weekends. The combination of sharp lemon and sweet crackle has made it a permanent fixture on cafe counters and kitchen tables across the country.
